newsitem.title: FINLAND: ICE HOCKEY-CANADA AND U.S. SET TO RENEW RIVALRY.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-CANADA AND U.S. SET TO RENEW RIVALRY.

text.p: Canada and the United States will renew what has become ice hockey's fiercest rivalry when they face off in a crucial round-robin match at the world championship on Thursday.
The game will mark the first time the two countries have clashed since the final of last September's inaugural World Cup which was won by the Americans and sent Canadians into despondency.
Their national pride dented by the Americanisation of the game they claim as their own, Canadians have been seething for an opportunity to get even.
"The sight of that American jersey seems to inspire the guys a little more now," said Canadian coach Andy Murray after watching his team struggle to a 3-3 draw against Latvia on Wednesday.
"The Americans have obviously replaced the Soviets now as far as that old rivalry and feeling goes."
The game will feature two completely different teams from those that met at the World Cup.

While the World Cup featured the cream of the NHL crop with superstars such Wayne Gretzky and Eric Lindros, the world championship line-ups comprise players from teams who rashed out of the Stanley Cup playoffs.
It is unlikely that any players on either the U.S. and Canadian world championship squads will be on the ice at the Nagano Olympics, where professionals will play for the first time.

While the players will be different the emotion is expected to be the same. The Canadians are eager to re-establish themselves as the game's dominant force and the Americans equally anxious to add to their World Cup success by claiming their first world title in 64 years.
"You can't get over-emotional about these games," said Jackson, playing down the clash. "I don't want to blow this out of proportion.
"You can't make a bigger deal about this game than the one we just played or the one we will play on Saturday.
"But saying that, these guys play against each other all season and some of them are even team mates, so that internal rivalry is always going to exist."
Since their World Cup win, American confidence has grown and, Jackson says, so has Canadian respect.
"I think we're slowly earning respect from Canada and our guys obviously respect them," said Jackson. "I'm concerned that sometimes we respect Canada too much."
